readerTitle: Nobody got fired for buying the safe choice
caseNote: 실제 기업에 얽힌 일화 (IBM 격언, 출처 불명) + 실제 연구 (Herbert Simon의 제한된 합리성) + 가상 적용 (B2B 회계 서비스, 물류창고 지게차 배터리)
insight: 고객의 선택이 비합리적으로 보이면, 그 선택을 합리적으로 만드는 보이지 않는 제약과 동기가 무엇인지 먼저 찾는다.
misconception: 고객이 더 싸고 더 좋은 제안을 거절하면 편향이나 습관 때문이고, 그러니 설득하거나 가격을 더 내리면 된다.

sources.text: Simon, H. A. (1955). A Behavioral Model of Rational Choice. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 69(1).
Simon, H. A. (1956). Rational Choice and the Structure of the Environment. Psychological Review, 63(2).
The Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences 1978, Herbert A. Simon (nobelprize.org)
"Nobody ever got fired for buying IBM": 기업 구매 담당자 사이에 퍼진 격언. 최초 출처는 확인되지 않음

factChecks.note: "Nobody ever got fired for buying IBM" 격언은 최초 발언자와 시점이 확인되지 않습니다. 카드에서는 출처 불명의 격언(일화)으로만 표현했습니다. IBM이 경쟁사보다 비쌌다는 일반 서술은 구체 수치 없이 "often"으로 완화했습니다.
Herbert Simon의 1978년 노벨 경제학상 수상, 'satisficing'(satisfy + suffice) 용어 사용(1956년 논문)을 게시 전 다시 확인하세요.
B2B 회계 서비스와 창고 지게차 배터리 사례는 설명용 가상 사례이며 수치(25% 저렴 등)도 가정입니다.

cards.title: Nobody got fired for buying the safe choice
body: In the mainframe era, a saying spread among corporate buyers: *"Nobody ever got fired for buying IBM."* Nobody knows for sure who said it first.
IBM was often not the cheapest option. Yet many buyers kept choosing it. From the outside, that looks like paying extra for a logo. From the buyer's chair, it looked very different.

image.label: A buyer at a desk choosing between a familiar blue box and a cheaper unknown box
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 사무실 책상에 앉은 구매 담당자가 두 개의 상자 앞에서 고민. 왼쪽은 익숙한 파란 상자(가격표 높음), 오른쪽은 낯선 회색 상자(가격표 낮음). 담당자 뒤 벽에 상사의 그림자. 실제 기업 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: They picked the pricier firm. Why?
body: You run a mid-sized accounting firm. A company's finance manager compared your audit proposal with one from a famous large firm. Yours was about 25% cheaper and, by their own feedback, more detailed.
They chose the large firm anyway. What's the most useful way to read this?

options.text: Brand bias. People overvalue big names, so there's little you can do
options.feedback: It's a comforting story, but it ends your learning. You lose the chance to find a reason you could actually address.

options.text: The manager carries the risk if a small firm fails. Lower that risk for them
options.feedback: This treats the choice as sensible from where the manager sits. It points to fixes like references, a phased start or guarantees.

options.text: Price wasn't low enough. Cut it further next time
options.feedback: Price matters, but you were already cheaper. A deeper cut shrinks your margin without touching the real worry.

cards.title: The savings go to the company. The risk goes to the buyer.
body: Think about who gains and who loses. If the cheaper supplier works, the company saves money and the buyer gets little credit. If it fails, the buyer gets the blame.
If the famous supplier fails, the buyer can say, "We chose the industry leader." That protects their job.
So the IBM saying isn't about foolish buyers. It describes **a sensible choice for the person deciding**, even when it isn't the cheapest choice for the company.

cards.title: Bounded rationality
body: The economist Herbert Simon called it **bounded rationality**: people decide with limited time, limited information and their own goals. Within those limits, a choice that seems odd can be reasonable.

Simon also used the word *satisficing*: picking the first option that is good enough, because searching for the best costs effort too. His work on decision-making earned him the 1978 Nobel Prize in economics.

image.label: A person inside a circle of limits: time, information, personal risk
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 가운데 의사결정자 인물, 주변을 원형 울타리가 둘러싸고 울타리 판자마다 "Time", "Information", "Personal risk", "Switching cost", "Attention" 라벨. 울타리 안에서 가장 가까운 문을 고르는 모습.

cards.title: Where the hidden reasons usually live
body: When a customer's choice puzzles you, check these first:
list: **Personal risk:** who gets blamed if it goes wrong
**Cost of finding out:** comparing options takes time they don't have
**Missing information:** they know something about their situation that you don't
**Other goals:** their boss, their team, their schedule
cards.callout: "Irrational" often means "reasons I can't see yet."
cards.softwareNote: A team keeps exporting your dashboard to a spreadsheet instead of using it. Maybe their manager only reads spreadsheets. The fix is a better export, not a lecture.

cards.title: Real mistakes exist too.
body: Decades of research show people do make predictable errors. They misjudge odds, overweight what's vivid and stick with defaults. Not every odd choice hides a good reason.

And a choice can be sensible for the person yet still hurt them or their company. The goal isn't to excuse every behavior. It's to ask "what would make this sensible?" before you decide it's a bias. Then test your guess, rather than assuming it.

cards.title: Now it's a warehouse.
body: You sell a new forklift battery system. Your numbers show it costs less over five years than the old batteries. The warehouse manager likes the numbers but won't switch.
Their bonus depends on shipping every order on time. What do you do?

options.text: Send a clearer report showing the five-year savings
options.feedback: Clear numbers help, but the savings were never the doubt. It doesn't touch the manager's fear of a missed shipment.

options.text: Offer a trial on one shift, with your technician on site and a quick swap back
options.feedback: This lowers the risk the manager personally carries. You spend more on the trial but give them a safe way to say yes.

options.text: Conclude they're stuck in old habits and move on
options.feedback: You save time, but you misread a reasonable fear as stubbornness and leave a winnable deal behind.

cards.softwareNote: The same holds when selling software to operations teams. An IT lead who fears a failed rollout will often choose a pilot with one team over a cheaper company-wide deal.

cards.title: Before calling a customer irrational, find what makes their choice sensible.
body: Most puzzling choices make sense once you see the person's limits and risks. Fix those, and the choice often changes.
**Try it today:** recall a customer who said no to something you thought was clearly better. Write down one personal risk or cost they faced that your offer ignored.
